analysis.one_liner: Bans shrimp imports from countries whose food inspection systems the FDA finds not equivalent.
analysis.headline: Referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on May 13, 2025, where it has sat without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require the FDA to negotiate inspection agreements with every country that ships shrimp to the United States, and would refuse entry to shrimp from any country without such an agreement or without an inspection system the FDA deems equivalent for shrimp. Shrimp from noncompliant countries would be treated as adulterated and kept out of U.S. commerce. The sponsor represents a Gulf Coast shrimp district; the bill would shield domestic shrimpers from the roughly 90%-imported U.S. shrimp supply while raising a food-safety bar for foreign producers.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, Americans who eat shrimp would get a stronger safety guarantee on imported shrimp, since shipments from countries with weak or uninspected systems would be barred. Domestic Gulf shrimp fishermen and processors, concentrated in Mississippi, Louisiana, and Alabama, would gain the most economically: with most foreign sources cut off or forced into costly compliance, the domestic share of the market and prices for the domestic catch would rise.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gulf shrimp fishermen and U.S. shrimp eaters

how_it_helps.text: Within one year of enactment, shrimp would be refused admission if it comes from a country that has not signed an FDA inspection agreement or whose shrimp-inspection system is not equivalent to the FDA's, including adequate staffing and enforcement of growing and transport conditions [S2][S3].
Shrimp from a noncompliant country would be deemed adulterated under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, keeping it out of interstate commerce [S2][S3].
The FDA must seek inspection agreements with every country that has a registered facility shipping shrimp to the U.S., and report to Congress annually on implementation [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Shrimp importers and the exporting countries that supply most U.S. shrimp would bear compliance costs or lose market access, and consumers would likely pay more at the grocery store and in restaurants, since shrimp is the most-consumed seafood in America and the vast majority of it is imported. Foreign governments would face the burden of proving their systems equivalent and opening facilities to FDA inspection.

drawbacks.text: An equivalency-and-agreement requirement covering every shrimp-exporting country could function as a near-ban on imports, and with the U.S. importing the large majority of its shrimp, prices for consumers could rise sharply [S2][S3].

The bill gives the FDA no new inspection funding or staffing; the U.S. already inspects only a small share of foreign food facilities, so the equivalency determinations and overseas inspections the bill demands may outpace the agency's capacity.

Import bans framed as safety measures can double as trade protection; whether foreign systems genuinely fail the equivalency test, or simply get locked out, would rest largely on FDA discretion with annual reports as the only oversight [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The food-safety goal is real — imported shrimp has repeatedly been flagged for banned antibiotics and un-inspected facilities — and the bill creates a clear, enforceable standard rather than relying on port-by-port testing. But the economic cost lands on the same ordinary consumers the safety rule protects: shrimp is a staple protein for many households, and a rule that most exporting countries cannot or will not meet would raise its price. The bill would have been stronger with dedicated FDA funding to actually perform the inspections it requires.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has received no hearing, no markup, and no vote so far in this Congress.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Ezell of Mississippi introduced the bill on May 13, 2025, joined as original cosponsors by Rep. Carter of Louisiana and Rep. Letlow of Louisiana — all Gulf Coast members [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, which is the chamber with jurisdiction over the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act [S1][S5].
Five members have cosponsored the bill — four Republicans and one Democrat [S4].
No further action has been taken since the referral, according to the complete action history [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No outcome yet: the U.S. shrimp-import status quo — largely uninspected foreign supply and a struggling domestic fleet — continues while the bill sits in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill is stalled in committee

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and four of five cosponsors are Republicans, with one Democratic cosponsor; no member has spoken or voted against it, and no committee action has occurred to reveal opposition.

industries.industry: Gulf Coast shrimp fishermen and domestic processors
industries.note: The import ban would shrink the foreign supply that dominates the U.S. market, lifting demand and prices for the domestic catch. The same restriction, however, would raise shrimp prices for American consumers, so the industry's gain comes partly at shoppers' expense.

industries.industry: Shrimp importers and foreign exporting countries (e.g., India, Ecuador, Vietnam, Indonesia)
industries.note: Exporters would have to win FDA equivalency determinations and open facilities to U.S. inspection or lose access to the U.S. market entirely. Any access lost would come out of the American shrimp supply, pushing prices up for consumers.
Retailers and restaurants would face higher and less reliable shrimp supply, but a credibly enforced safety standard could reduce the risk of adulterated product reaching their shelves.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has the profile of most private members' bills: a single-chamber referral, five cosponsors, and no committee activity for months. Unless the Energy and Commerce Committee schedules a markup or the provision is attached to a larger food- or farm-related package, it will likely die quietly at the end of the 119th Congress. Gulf Coast members periodically reintroduce versions of this idea, so a future Congress could see it again.
